title: Packing tokens for APIs — rough tricks
content:
Quick brain-dump about a handful of cheap/fast heuristics for pricing and packaging that try to capture the savings we get from packing calls together (batching, prefix caching) without forcing customers into heavy engineering work. Keep it informal — testing hypotheses.

Goal
- Convert backend serving efficiencies (batching, KV cache hits, session amortization) into simple product-level levers (credits, tokens, sessions) that are intuitive for devs.
- Provide defensible unit economics to sales for hybrid offers (small commit + burst credits).

Core assumptions (pull these into a canonical spreadsheet later)
- GPU cost (fully burdened, infra+ops): $2.40 / GPU-hour (example for mixed A100/RTX pools). Replace with dedicated numbers per customer.
- Useful token throughput per GPU-hour (in practice): ~120M tokens/hour for medium-length gen workloads (amortized across batching, KV cache effects). Range 80–180M depending on model & sequence length.
- Baseline per-token infra cost ~= $2.40 / 120M = $0.00000002 / token (~2e-8 USD). Call it 2e-8 as the kernel.
- Add overheads (control plane, storage, SRE, margin): multiply by 4–8 depending on offering. So billable baseline per-token is ~8e-8 to 1.6e-7.
- Latency premium: low-latency paths (no batching) cost ~3–5x more in practice; good to surface as an option.

Simple heuristics to expose savings
1) Packing window credits
- Idea: Expose a "packing window" that encourages clients to batch several user interactions into a single request when UX allows. Customers buy credits that are consumed per packed API call rather than per token, or get a discounted per-token rate for calls flagged as batched.
- Implementation (product): Add an optional header/showing flag: X-Pack-Window: 200ms or client groups n user inputs into a single request. Server measures and applies a discount when average token-per-request > threshold.
- Pricing front: if a single call bundles 3 microcalls (3x tokens) but avoids repeated KV overhead and increases batching, we can offer 25–40% discount on infra-billable tokens for that call.
- Rough calc: if packing increases effective tokens/hour from 120M to 150M (25% uplift), unit cost drops from 2e-8 to 1.6e-8. After overhead multiplier, that's a visible 20–30% saving.

2) Session amortization credits
- Idea: Treat a session as a tiny monthly resource pool: e.g., allocate X free warm-up tokens per session to cover KV cache priming and short prompts. Useful for chat apps where the first few exchanges are costlier.
- Heuristic: first 500 tokens / session charged at 0.5x unit-rate (or free up to a cap for starter plans). This is a blunt lever but aligns incentives: keep sessions active rather than re-open repeatedly.
- Back-of-envelope: if priming costs ~20% of session tokens on average, this credit reduces apparent cost per session and raises perceived value for interactive apps.

3) Microburst credits + expiry
- Idea: Sell tiny burst packs (e.g., 50k tokens) that are time-limited (30–90 days) and priced with a small premium vs committed tokens. Serves starup growth and ephemeral experiments.
- Pricing suggestion: committed tokens (annual) = baseline unit price * 1.0; 30-day bursts = baseline * 1.35; one-off payg = baseline * 1.6.
- Rationale: we monetize impatience while giving customers a clear migration path to commits.

4) Per-route latency-aware multipliers
- Idea: Let customers opt a route for latency SLO. If they choose "interactive" SLO, we route to faster paths and apply a latency multiplier (x1.8–x3) on per-token price. If they choose "economy", route through aggressive batching and give discount.
- Product benefit: transparent tradeoff between user-perceived latency and unit economics. Useful for enterprise contracts.

Example role-of-quantization and model variants
- Offer cheaper model variants (q4/q8) as "economy" model in catalog. Present as: "redwood-economy-1" = 0.7x tokens cost, "redwood-interactive-1" = 1.0x, "redwood-low-latency-pro" = 1.6x.
- Combine with routing policies and credits: e.g., committed customers can pin interactive variants but get a small discount on economy during off-peak windows.

Packaging sketches (try to keep simple)
- Starter dev: 100k tokens/mo free credits, microburst packs at 30-day expiry, per-token payg at baseline*1.6. (Target: viral PLG onboarding.)
- Interactive payg: per-token baseline price, optional "packing window" discount of -25% if >avg tokens/request threshold.
- Team committed: monthly committed tokens at baseline *0.85, includes session credits (500 tokens/session) and 3 microburst packs included for on-demand.
- Enterprise SLA: dedicated pools, latency multiplier options, reserved throughput with per-hour minimums.

Short examples
- If we sell a microburst 50k pack at $5 (=> $0.0001 / token), but our baseline unit cost is 8e-8, there's huge margin on bursts. That's fine because bursts carry no commitment; we should allocate some % to cover provisioning and oversubscription risk.
- A team with 10k interactive daily active users, 5 msgs/day, avg 200 tokens/msg => 10k *5*200=10M tokens/day -> 300M tokens/mo. With baseline ~8e-8 -> infra cost ~$24/mo. Selling committed tokens at baseline*0.85 ~ $0.000000068/token => $20.4/mo. Shows committed discounts can be small in $ but meaningful at scale.

Open questions / TODOs
- Validate the 120M tokens/hour assumption across our actual model mix and sequence length distributions (need model-by-model numbers). Add per-model token-throughput table.
- How to measure packing window reliably without introducing fraud (clients faking flags). We need server-side detection (tokens/request distribution, call-per-user patterns) and a fraud budget.
- UX: how to show packing incentives to developers clearly in docs and SDKs (javascript/py client helpers?).
- Accounting: ensure microburst expiries can be enforced and UI shows remaining days clearly.
- Sales playbook: define thresholds where we prefer to move customers from bursts -> commit.

Immediate next steps
- Run a query on our serving logs: distribution of tokens/request, average KV cache hit after 1/5/10 exchanges, and effective tokens/hour per GPU per model. (Benji to run.)
- Prototype server-side packing-detection heuristic and run against 2 weeks of traffic to estimate uplift. (Aisha to prod.)
- Draft short dev-facing SDK helpers that batch calls in browser/node: two methods crumbed into quickstart.

Random notes / heuristics
- Prefer percent-based discounts for packaging (easier to explain than weird per-call credit math).
- Keep credit expiries visible; expiration drives conversions but pisses off some users. 30 days is reasonable default.
- Where possible present both token-equivalent and dollar-equivalent in portal to avoid confusion.

"Things I might try in a playtest"
- Offer a "pack-and-save" toggle: if enabled, client auto-batches small prompts in a 150ms window and shows users that they saved X% on the last message. Track conversion.
- Offer 'session warmers' for 0.1c per session that guarantees warm KV cache for next N requests (sales ask for this sometimes).

End of notes. This is intentionally messy — will refine into a short brief once we have logs and model-throughput numbers.
